questions.q: A patient with severe unipolar major depression remits after a successful acute course of bilateral ECT. What clinical question did the CORE continuation ECT trial primarily address?

o.t: Whether continuation ECT could prevent depressive relapse after acute ECT response
o.fb: The trial focused on relapse prevention after remission with acute ECT, not on proving acute ECT efficacy.

o.t: Whether unilateral ECT was superior to bilateral ECT for acute mania
o.fb: The study enrolled patients with unipolar depression who had already remitted with bilateral ECT.

o.t: Whether ECT should replace all antidepressant pharmacotherapy in outpatient depression
o.fb: The study compared two continuation strategies after ECT remission and did not argue that ECT should replace all medication treatment.

o.t: Whether maintenance psychotherapy alone was sufficient after psychotic depression
o.fb: Psychotherapy alone was not the tested continuation strategy in this trial.

questions.q: In the Kellner 2006 trial, continuation ECT was most directly compared with which relapse-prevention strategy?

o.t: Lithium plus nortriptyline continuation pharmacotherapy
o.fb: The pharmacotherapy arm used lithium carbonate plus nortriptyline as an active comparator.

o.t: Placebo-only follow-up after abrupt discontinuation
o.fb: The trial compared two active continuation treatments rather than using placebo-only discontinuation.

o.t: Cognitive behavioral therapy delivered weekly for one year
o.fb: CBT was not the continuation comparator in the CORE ECT relapse-prevention study.

o.t: Clozapine augmentation for treatment-resistant depression
o.fb: Clozapine was not part of the continuation strategy tested in this depression trial.

questions.q: Which teaching point best captures the clinical bottom line of the Kellner continuation ECT study?

o.t: Relapse prevention is still needed after ECT remission, and continuation ECT is a reasonable active strategy for selected patients.
o.fb: The study highlights that ECT response is not the endpoint; patients need an active continuation plan.

o.t: Patients who remit with ECT can usually stop all treatment without close monitoring.
o.fb: Relapse after ECT remission remains a major risk, so stopping treatment without a plan is unsafe.

o.t: Continuation ECT is only appropriate for schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
o.fb: This trial studied relapse prevention in major depression after acute ECT response.

o.t: Lithium and nortriptyline were shown to be ineffective as continuation treatment.
o.fb: The pharmacotherapy arm was an active comparator and was not shown to be ineffective.

questions.q: A student asks why the trial matters if ECT is already known to work acutely. What is the best response?

o.t: Acute response and sustained remission are different outcomes, and this trial studied the continuation phase.
o.fb: The key distinction is acute symptom improvement versus preventing relapse over months after remission.

o.t: The trial was designed to show that acute ECT has no meaningful antidepressant effect.
o.fb: The trial assumed acute ECT can be effective and asked what should happen after remission.

o.t: The trial mainly tested whether ECT causes serotonin syndrome.
o.fb: Serotonin syndrome was not the clinical question in this continuation-treatment study.

o.t: The trial only measured patient preference and did not assess depressive relapse.
o.fb: Relapse of depression was the central outcome.

questions.q: Which patient would most closely match the population studied in Kellner 2006?

o.t: An adult with DSM-IV unipolar depression who remitted after a course of bilateral ECT
o.fb: The study randomized adults with unipolar depression after remission with bilateral ECT.

o.t: A child with ADHD beginning stimulant treatment for the first time
o.fb: The trial was not about ADHD or pediatric stimulant treatment.

o.t: A patient with schizophrenia beginning clozapine for persistent hallucinations
o.fb: The diagnosis and treatment phase do not match this depression continuation trial.

o.t: A person with opioid use disorder choosing between methadone and buprenorphine
o.fb: The trial was unrelated to medication treatment for opioid use disorder.

questions.q: A patient who has taken paroxetine for several years wants to stop quickly because she feels better. Which counseling point best reflects the clinical lesson of antidepressant withdrawal literature?

o.t: Discontinuation symptoms can occur, so stopping should usually be planned, gradual, and monitored.
o.fb: The core teaching point is informed consent, tapering, and follow-up rather than abrupt cessation.

o.t: Withdrawal symptoms prove that the original depression was misdiagnosed.
o.fb: Withdrawal can occur after physiologic adaptation and does not by itself prove the original diagnosis was wrong.

o.t: All antidepressants must be continued lifelong once started.
o.fb: Long-term treatment decisions should be individualized; withdrawal risk does not mean indefinite treatment is mandatory for everyone.

o.t: Patients should stop abruptly so relapse can be distinguished from medication effects.
o.fb: Abrupt stopping can worsen discontinuation symptoms and is generally not a safe diagnostic strategy.

questions.q: Which symptom cluster is most consistent with antidepressant discontinuation rather than a simple return of baseline depression?

o.t: Dizziness, electric-shock sensations, nausea, insomnia, and anxiety soon after dose reduction
o.fb: Neurologic and flu-like symptoms emerging after dose reduction are classic discontinuation clues.

o.t: Months of isolated low mood beginning before any medication change
o.fb: Symptoms predating a dose change are less suggestive of withdrawal.

o.t: Progressive memory loss with focal neurologic deficits
o.fb: That pattern requires a neurologic workup and is not typical antidepressant discontinuation.

o.t: Persistent euphoria with decreased need for sleep before antidepressant exposure
o.fb: That presentation suggests possible mania or hypomania rather than antidepressant withdrawal.

questions.q: A shelf-style question asks how to distinguish antidepressant withdrawal from depressive relapse. Which feature favors withdrawal?

o.t: A close temporal relationship to missed doses or dose reduction
o.fb: Withdrawal symptoms often begin soon after a medication reduction or interruption.

o.t: Symptoms that began years before the antidepressant was prescribed
o.fb: Symptoms that predate medication exposure do not support withdrawal.

o.t: Absence of any physical or neurologic symptoms after stopping
o.fb: Physical symptoms are often an important clue when present, though withdrawal can still vary.

o.t: A clear manic episode with psychosis during continued full-dose treatment
o.fb: Mania with psychosis requires a different diagnostic and safety assessment.

questions.q: Which clinical approach best avoids overinterpreting the Moncrieff withdrawal discussion?

o.t: Discuss benefits, adverse effects, withdrawal risk, and patient goals before changing treatment.
o.fb: Balanced shared decision-making is the practical takeaway for students and clinicians.

o.t: Tell patients antidepressants never help and should not be prescribed.
o.fb: Withdrawal concerns do not prove that antidepressants are never useful.

o.t: Tell patients discontinuation symptoms are always imaginary.
o.fb: Discontinuation symptoms are clinically recognized and should be taken seriously.

o.t: Use withdrawal symptoms as a reason to avoid follow-up appointments.
o.fb: Follow-up is especially important when tapering medications.

questions.q: A patient asks why tapering may become slower at lower antidepressant doses. Which explanation is most appropriate?

o.t: Small milligram changes near the low end can still produce meaningful changes in receptor occupancy for some drugs.
o.fb: This is the rationale behind slower or hyperbolic tapering for selected long-term users.

o.t: Lower doses are always pharmacologically inactive and can be skipped.
o.fb: Low doses can still have biologic effects, especially for some serotonergic medications.

o.t: Tapering speed should be identical for every patient and every antidepressant.
o.fb: Tapering should account for the medication, duration of use, symptoms, and patient preference.

o.t: The goal is to provoke withdrawal so the patient learns to tolerate it.
o.fb: The goal is to reduce avoidable suffering and maintain clinical stability.

questions.q: Brown's expressed emotion work is most important for linking which family-level observation to schizophrenia relapse risk?

o.t: High criticism, hostility, or emotional overinvolvement in close relatives
o.fb: Expressed emotion refers to these relational features and their association with relapse risk.

o.t: Family income alone as the main cause of schizophrenia
o.fb: Socioeconomic context matters, but expressed emotion specifically concerns family emotional climate.

o.t: The number of siblings as a direct diagnostic criterion
o.fb: Sibling count is not the expressed emotion construct.

o.t: A patient's preference for individual rather than group therapy
o.fb: Treatment preference is not what Brown's expressed emotion construct measured.

questions.q: Which vignette best illustrates a high expressed emotion environment?

o.t: A parent repeatedly criticizes the patient as lazy and intrudes intensely into every daily decision.
o.fb: Criticism plus emotional overinvolvement captures the high expressed emotion pattern.

o.t: A sibling asks the patient what support would feel useful after discharge.
o.fb: Collaborative support is not high expressed emotion.

o.t: A relative attends psychoeducation and practices calm communication.
o.fb: Psychoeducation and calm communication are interventions that can reduce relapse risk.

o.t: A family member maintains respectful distance while ensuring medication access.
o.fb: Respectful support does not fit the high criticism or overinvolvement pattern.

questions.q: What is the best clinical use of expressed emotion research for an MS3 on an inpatient psychiatry rotation?

o.t: Assess family stress and communication patterns when planning relapse prevention.
o.fb: The finding makes family climate a practical relapse-prevention target.

o.t: Tell families they caused the patient's schizophrenia.
o.fb: Expressed emotion is a relapse-risk construct, not a blame-based cause of schizophrenia.

o.t: Exclude families from discharge planning whenever psychosis is present.
o.fb: The research supports thoughtful family intervention, not automatic exclusion.

o.t: Use expressed emotion as a stand-alone diagnostic test for schizophrenia.
o.fb: Expressed emotion is not a diagnostic test.

questions.q: Which intervention follows most directly from the expressed emotion literature?

o.t: Family psychoeducation that reduces criticism and improves problem-solving
o.fb: Later family-intervention trials built on expressed emotion by targeting communication and stress.

o.t: Stopping antipsychotic medication in all patients with supportive families
o.fb: Family intervention is an adjunct to evidence-based treatment, not a reason to stop indicated medication.

o.t: Using confrontation to prove that relatives are wrong
o.fb: Blaming relatives is countertherapeutic and misses the collaborative prevention goal.

o.t: Replacing all outpatient care with genetic testing
o.fb: The expressed emotion construct concerns social environment, not genetic testing.

questions.q: Which statement best avoids a common misunderstanding of Brown's work?

o.t: High expressed emotion predicts relapse risk in a stress-vulnerability framework; it does not mean families caused the illness.
o.fb: This preserves the clinical importance of the finding without blaming families.

o.t: High expressed emotion is the only proven cause of schizophrenia.
o.fb: Schizophrenia is multifactorial and expressed emotion is not a sole cause.

o.t: Expressed emotion is irrelevant once antipsychotics are prescribed.
o.fb: Family emotional climate can still affect relapse risk even when medication is used.

o.t: Low expressed emotion means a patient no longer needs outpatient follow-up.
o.fb: Supportive family climate does not replace clinical follow-up.

questions.q: Leff's 1982 controlled trial selected families of patients with schizophrenia at particularly high relapse risk based on which feature?

o.t: High contact with high expressed emotion relatives
o.fb: The study targeted patients living in close contact with relatives whose expressed emotion was high.

o.t: Absence of any family involvement after discharge
o.fb: The key risk context was high-contact, high-expressed-emotion family involvement.

o.t: A genetic test confirming complement activation
o.fb: Complement genetics belongs to later schizophrenia research, not this family-intervention trial.

o.t: Treatment resistance after clozapine failure
o.fb: The trial focused on family social intervention while patients remained on neuroleptic medication.

questions.q: Which components best describe the Leff family intervention package?

o.t: Education about schizophrenia, a relatives group, and family sessions with relatives and patients
o.fb: These components aimed to reduce stress and improve family coping.

o.t: A medication-free inpatient detoxification protocol
o.fb: Patients were maintained on neuroleptic medication; the intervention was psychosocial.

o.t: Exposure therapy for trauma memories delivered without family involvement
o.fb: The study tested family social intervention, not trauma-focused exposure.

o.t: A diagnostic interview designed to replace DSM criteria
o.fb: The trial was not a diagnostic-validity study.

questions.q: What result made Leff 1982 a landmark for family psychoeducation in schizophrenia?

o.t: Relapse was lower in the family-intervention group than in routine outpatient care.
o.fb: The trial showed that a structured family intervention could reduce relapse risk.

o.t: Medication adherence became irrelevant after one family meeting.
o.fb: The intervention was delivered alongside neuroleptic maintenance, not as a replacement.

o.t: Family therapy worsened outcomes compared with no contact.
o.fb: The landmark finding was a relapse-prevention benefit, not harm.

o.t: The trial showed that schizophrenia is caused by parenting style.
o.fb: The study supports relapse prevention through family intervention, not a parent-blaming etiology.

questions.q: A student asks why all patients in the Leff trial stayed on neuroleptics. What is the best answer?

o.t: The study tested whether family intervention added benefit to medication-based care.
o.fb: Keeping medication in place helped isolate the added value of psychosocial family work.

o.t: The study was designed to prove neuroleptics have no role in relapse prevention.
o.fb: The design did not attempt to remove medication from relapse prevention.

o.t: Neuroleptics were used only as placebo tablets.
o.fb: Patients received active neuroleptic maintenance.

o.t: Medication status was unrelated to the family intervention question.
o.fb: Medication status matters because the family intervention was an adjunctive strategy.

questions.q: Which discharge-planning recommendation is most consistent with Leff 1982?

o.t: Offer structured family psychoeducation when a patient with schizophrenia returns to a high-stress household.
o.fb: The trial supports family education and support as relapse-prevention tools in high-risk family settings.

o.t: Avoid asking about family contact because it is not clinically relevant.
o.fb: Family contact and communication are directly relevant to relapse prevention.

o.t: Use family criticism as proof that the patient cannot live in the community.
o.fb: High expressed emotion signals a need for intervention, not automatic exclusion from community care.

o.t: Replace relapse planning with a one-time printed medication handout.
o.fb: The intervention was more active and relational than a single handout.

questions.q: Falloon's family management trial in schizophrenia most directly compared at-home family therapy with which control condition?

o.t: Clinic-based individual supportive care while patients continued neuroleptic maintenance
o.fb: The comparison tested family management against individual supportive community care with medication maintained.

o.t: Long-term inpatient hospitalization without medication
o.fb: The control was community-based supportive care, not medication-free hospitalization.

o.t: Ketamine infusion for treatment-resistant depression
o.fb: The trial was about schizophrenia relapse prevention through family management.

o.t: A genetics-only risk disclosure session
o.fb: The intervention involved education and behavioral problem-solving, not genetic disclosure.

questions.q: Which skill was central to the Falloon family management approach?

o.t: Training families in behavioral problem-solving and stress reduction
o.fb: The intervention aimed to improve understanding of illness and reduce family stress through practical skills.

o.t: Teaching families to challenge delusions directly until the patient agrees
o.fb: Confrontational correction is not the family management strategy tested.

o.t: Removing all relatives from treatment planning
o.fb: The model intentionally brought family members into the relapse-prevention plan.

o.t: Using family therapy only after relapse has already occurred
o.fb: The trial was prevention-focused and community-based.

questions.q: What was the main outcome pattern reported in Falloon 1982?

o.t: Family management reduced major symptomatic exacerbations compared with supportive individual care.
o.fb: The study found fewer relapses in the family-treated group.

o.t: Family management increased relapse by increasing contact with relatives.
o.fb: The structured intervention was associated with reduced, not increased, relapse.

o.t: Supportive individual care eliminated the need for medication monitoring.
o.fb: Medication maintenance remained part of care in the trial.

o.t: No patient in either group had any psychotic symptoms during follow-up.
o.fb: The trial compared relapse risk; it did not show complete absence of symptoms for all participants.

questions.q: A resident says family intervention works only by making relatives less emotional. Which response is most accurate for Falloon's model?

o.t: It also teaches concrete communication and problem-solving skills that reduce day-to-day stress.
o.fb: Falloon's approach was behavioral and skills-based, not merely emotional ventilation.

o.t: It works by proving relatives are responsible for schizophrenia.
o.fb: The model does not assign causal blame to relatives.

o.t: It works by replacing antipsychotics with family meetings.
o.fb: Patients remained on neuroleptic maintenance medication.

o.t: It works only for patients with no family conflict.
o.fb: The intervention was designed for families where stress and communication problems matter clinically.

questions.q: Which MS3-level discharge plan best reflects Falloon 1982?

o.t: Combine medication follow-up with family education, communication practice, and relapse-warning planning.
o.fb: The study supports integrating pharmacologic and family-management strategies.

o.t: Give a one-page handout and avoid family sessions because they may increase relapse.
o.fb: Structured family sessions were the active ingredient, not something to avoid by default.

o.t: Use family conflict as a reason to discharge without outpatient services.
o.fb: Family stress should trigger more careful relapse-prevention planning.

o.t: Focus only on diagnostic validity and defer treatment planning.
o.fb: Falloon's work is a treatment-planning study, not a diagnostic-validity framework.

questions.q: McFarlane 1995 compared which two psychoeducational formats for schizophrenia?

o.t: Multiple-family group treatment versus single-family psychoeducational treatment
o.fb: The key comparison was whether a multifamily format improved outcomes beyond single-family work.

o.t: ECT versus lithium plus nortriptyline
o.fb: That comparison belongs to continuation treatment after ECT remission, not McFarlane's schizophrenia study.

o.t: Medication management versus placebo only
o.fb: The study compared psychosocial family formats rather than active medication versus placebo.

o.t: Individual psychodynamic therapy versus supportive care
o.fb: The intervention was family psychoeducation for schizophrenia.

questions.q: Which mechanism best explains why a multiple-family group might add value in schizophrenia relapse prevention?

o.t: Families learn problem-solving with peers and reduce isolation while practicing lower-stress communication.
o.fb: The multifamily format creates shared learning, support, and practical problem-solving opportunities.

o.t: Patients are encouraged to stop medication once the group begins.
o.fb: Family psychoeducation is an adjunct to ongoing clinical care, not a medication-discontinuation strategy.

o.t: The group prevents relapse by diagnosing schizophrenia without symptoms.
o.fb: The trial focused on treatment outcomes, not diagnostic replacement.

o.t: Relatives are trained to confront hallucinations until insight is restored.
o.fb: Confrontational correction is not the therapeutic mechanism of psychoeducational multifamily work.

questions.q: What outcome made the McFarlane study clinically important?

o.t: Multiple-family groups produced lower relapse rates than single-family psychoeducation over follow-up.
o.fb: The study suggested that the group format can improve relapse-prevention outcomes.

o.t: Single-family treatment cured schizophrenia in all participants.
o.fb: The trial did not show cure; it studied relapse and functioning outcomes.

o.t: Psychoeducation was harmful compared with no treatment.
o.fb: The study supported psychoeducational family work rather than showing harm.

o.t: Medication adherence was irrelevant to relapse risk.
o.fb: Medication adherence remained clinically relevant in schizophrenia relapse prevention.

questions.q: Which patient population most closely matches the McFarlane 1995 trial?

o.t: Young adults with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders after an acute psychotic episode
o.fb: The study enrolled acutely psychotic patients with schizophrenia disorders and followed relapse outcomes.

o.t: Adolescents with suicidal ideation receiving attachment-based family therapy
o.fb: That population matches Diamond's ABFT trial, not McFarlane's schizophrenia study.

o.t: Adults with panic disorder receiving imipramine and CBT
o.fb: McFarlane 1995 was not a panic-disorder pharmacotherapy trial.

o.t: Children with ADHD randomized to stimulant titration protocols
o.fb: That describes the MTA ADHD trial rather than multifamily schizophrenia psychoeducation.

questions.q: A hospital wants to implement the McFarlane model. Which feature should be prioritized?

o.t: A structured, ongoing multifamily psychoeducation group with problem-solving practice
o.fb: The evidence is for structured, sustained psychoeducation rather than a single informal meeting.

o.t: A one-time lecture with no family interaction
o.fb: The intervention's value comes from ongoing family engagement and group learning.

o.t: A rule that patients cannot attend with relatives
o.fb: The model includes family participation as a core element.

o.t: A genetic counseling session replacing relapse-prevention planning
o.fb: Genetic counseling does not substitute for psychoeducational relapse prevention.

questions.q: Diamond 2010 tested Attachment-Based Family Therapy primarily in which clinical population?

o.t: Adolescents with suicidal ideation
o.fb: The trial evaluated ABFT as a family-based treatment for suicidal adolescents.

o.t: Older adults with delirium in the ICU
o.fb: That population belongs to delirium-prevention and delirium-detection studies, not ABFT.

o.t: Adults with treatment-resistant schizophrenia receiving clozapine
o.fb: ABFT was not a clozapine trial.

o.t: Children with ADHD receiving medication management
o.fb: That describes the MTA ADHD study, not Diamond's ABFT trial.

questions.q: What is the central therapeutic target of Attachment-Based Family Therapy?

o.t: Repairing attachment ruptures and improving parent-adolescent communication
o.fb: ABFT uses family work to strengthen attachment security and communication around distress.

o.t: Training the adolescent to avoid all family discussion of suicidal thoughts
o.fb: ABFT aims to make family communication safer, not to suppress discussion.

o.t: Replacing safety planning with genetic testing
o.fb: Genetic testing is not the core ABFT mechanism.

o.t: Teaching parents to confront the adolescent until symptoms stop
o.fb: ABFT emphasizes repair and emotional communication rather than confrontation.

questions.q: Which trial design feature best describes Diamond 2010?

o.t: A randomized comparison of ABFT with an enhanced usual-care condition
o.fb: The study used a randomized design to compare ABFT against enhanced usual care.

o.t: A qualitative case series with no comparison group
o.fb: The landmark study was a controlled trial, not only a case series.

o.t: A medication dose-finding trial for pediatric antidepressants
o.fb: The tested intervention was psychotherapy, not a medication titration.

o.t: A cross-sectional survey of adverse childhood experiences
o.fb: That design describes the ACE Study more closely than ABFT.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate clinical takeaway from ABFT for an MS3?

o.t: For some suicidal adolescents, a structured family-based therapy can be part of reducing suicidal ideation.
o.fb: ABFT shows that family repair can be a treatment target in adolescent suicidality.

o.t: Family therapy replaces acute suicide-risk assessment.
o.fb: Risk assessment and safety planning remain essential even when family therapy is used.

o.t: Parents should be excluded whenever suicidality is present.
o.fb: ABFT is built around carefully involving caregivers when clinically appropriate.

o.t: Suicidal ideation is best treated only with inpatient hospitalization.
o.fb: Hospitalization may be needed for acute safety, but outpatient family-based treatments can also be important.

questions.q: Which statement best avoids overclaiming Diamond 2010?

o.t: ABFT has evidence for reducing suicidal ideation, but it should be integrated with safety assessment and individualized care.
o.fb: This respects the trial's psychotherapy finding without ignoring acute safety needs.

o.t: ABFT eliminates the need to assess access to lethal means.
o.fb: Lethal-means assessment remains part of suicide-risk management.

o.t: ABFT proves that all adolescent suicidality is caused by parents.
o.fb: The therapy targets family attachment processes without assigning single-cause blame.

o.t: ABFT is a diagnostic test for borderline personality disorder.
o.fb: ABFT is a psychotherapy model, not a diagnostic instrument.

questions.q: Pinsof and Wynne's 1995 paper is best understood as what type of contribution?

o.t: An empirical overview of marital and family therapy evidence across conditions
o.fb: The paper synthesized the evidence base and offered conclusions and recommendations.

o.t: A single-site randomized medication trial for depression
o.fb: It was not a medication trial and did not focus on one pharmacologic intervention.

o.t: A genetic association study of schizophrenia
o.fb: Genetic association work is unrelated to this systemic-therapy overview.

o.t: A diagnostic-validity checklist for schizophrenia
o.fb: Diagnostic validity is associated with Robins and Guze, not Pinsof and Wynne.

questions.q: Which clinical principle best reflects a systemic therapy perspective?

o.t: Symptoms can be maintained or improved by patterns of interaction within relationships.
o.fb: Systemic models examine how relational patterns affect problems and recovery.

o.t: Only individual brain chemistry matters in psychiatric outcomes.
o.fb: A systemic approach explicitly includes relational and contextual processes.

o.t: Family members should never be included in treatment.
o.fb: Systemic therapy often uses family or couple participation as the treatment medium.

o.t: The therapist should ignore communication patterns and focus only on diagnosis codes.
o.fb: Communication patterns are a central target of marital and family therapy.

questions.q: What should an MS3 remember when applying the Pinsof and Wynne overview?

o.t: Family and couple interventions can be evidence-based when the relational context is clinically relevant.
o.fb: The paper supports using systemic interventions thoughtfully rather than viewing them as non-evidence-based.

o.t: All psychiatric disorders respond equally to the same family therapy protocol.
o.fb: The overview does not support a one-size-fits-all protocol for every condition.

o.t: Systemic therapy works only if medication is avoided.
o.fb: Systemic interventions can be combined with medication and other treatments.

o.t: Systemic therapy should be used only after every other treatment fails.
o.fb: Relational interventions can be first-line or adjunctive depending on the problem.

questions.q: Which outcome domain is especially important in systemic therapy research?

o.t: Relationship and family functioning in addition to individual symptoms
o.fb: Systemic treatment often aims to improve both individual distress and relational functioning.

o.t: Serum drug levels as the only valid endpoint
o.fb: Serum levels may matter in medication trials but not as the sole endpoint for family therapy.

o.t: Brain imaging findings without clinical outcomes
o.fb: Clinical and relational outcomes are central to therapy evaluation.

o.t: Length of hospitalization only, regardless of functioning
o.fb: Hospitalization may be relevant in some disorders, but systemic work also examines relational and symptom outcomes.

questions.q: Which statement best avoids a common overinterpretation of common systemic evidence?

o.t: Evidence for systemic therapy supports relational assessment, but treatment should still be matched to diagnosis, goals, and safety.
o.fb: This recognizes the evidence base while preserving individualized clinical judgment.

o.t: Family therapy evidence means individual therapy is obsolete.
o.fb: Different modalities have different indications and can complement one another.

o.t: A systemic formulation means the patient is not really ill.
o.fb: Relational context can matter even when a patient has a serious psychiatric illness.

o.t: Family therapy is useful only when all relatives agree on the problem.
o.fb: Disagreement itself may be a treatment target in systemic work.

questions.q: Minuchin's Psychosomatic Families is most closely associated with which therapy tradition?

o.t: Structural family therapy
o.fb: Minuchin's work examined family structure, boundaries, and interaction patterns.

o.t: Network meta-analysis of antidepressants
o.fb: Network meta-analysis is a quantitative evidence-synthesis method, not Minuchin's family model.

o.t: Candidate gene association testing
o.fb: Genetic association testing is unrelated to structural family therapy.

o.t: Continuation ECT relapse prevention
o.fb: ECT continuation treatment is a separate depression literature.

questions.q: Which pattern is classically described in Minuchin's psychosomatic family model?

o.t: Enmeshment, overprotectiveness, rigidity, and poor conflict resolution
o.fb: These family-structure patterns are central to the classic model.

o.t: Low expressed emotion and complete emotional disengagement in every case
o.fb: The model emphasizes enmeshment and overinvolvement rather than universal disengagement.

o.t: Absence of any family interaction around illness
o.fb: The model is specifically about interaction patterns around symptoms and family organization.

o.t: A single gene that determines psychosomatic illness
o.fb: Minuchin's framework is relational, not a single-gene model.

questions.q: What is the safest modern way to teach Minuchin's model to medical students?

o.t: As an influential relational formulation that can guide assessment without blaming families for illness
o.fb: The model is historically important but should be applied in a nonblaming, evidence-aware manner.

o.t: As proof that parents cause all somatic symptoms in children
o.fb: That is an overstatement and risks harmful blame.

o.t: As a reason to ignore biomedical evaluation
o.fb: Psychosomatic formulation should not replace appropriate medical assessment.

o.t: As a medication algorithm for schizophrenia relapse
o.fb: The model is not a schizophrenia medication algorithm.

questions.q: A child with chronic illness has escalating symptoms during family conflict. Which Minuchin-informed question is most useful?

o.t: How do family interactions, boundaries, and conflict responses change when symptoms appear?
o.fb: Structural family assessment looks at how symptoms and interaction patterns influence each other.

o.t: Which relative can be blamed for the child's symptoms?
o.fb: A blaming stance is not clinically helpful and misuses the model.

o.t: Can medical evaluation be stopped because this is a family problem?
o.fb: Medical and psychosocial assessment should be integrated.

o.t: Does the family have a serotonin transporter polymorphism?
o.fb: That question belongs to a different literature and does not assess family structure.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes Minuchin 1978 from later randomized family-intervention trials in schizophrenia?

o.t: Minuchin offered a structural family model; later schizophrenia trials tested relapse-prevention interventions empirically.
o.fb: This distinction separates theory-building from controlled outcome testing.

o.t: Minuchin conducted the largest antipsychotic effectiveness trial.
o.fb: That describes CATIE, not Psychosomatic Families.

o.t: Minuchin discovered complement C4 risk alleles.
o.fb: Complement C4 findings came from later schizophrenia genetics research.

o.t: Minuchin created the four-abilities model of treatment capacity.
o.fb: The four-abilities capacity model is associated with Appelbaum and Grisso.

questions.q: The London Depression Intervention Trial focused on depressed patients with which relational context?

o.t: Living with a critical partner
o.fb: The trial was grounded in the observation that partner criticism is linked with depressive relapse.

o.t: No current intimate relationship and no family contact
o.fb: The intervention specifically required a partner relationship context.

o.t: A parent with high expressed emotion toward a patient with schizophrenia
o.fb: That context fits schizophrenia family-intervention studies, not this depression couple-therapy trial.

o.t: A child with ADHD and school impairment
o.fb: The MTA study, not Leff 2000, addressed ADHD treatment strategies.

questions.q: What were the main active treatments compared in Leff 2000?

o.t: Couple therapy versus antidepressant medication treatment
o.fb: The trial compared a relational psychotherapy approach with antidepressant drug treatment.

o.t: ECT versus continuation pharmacotherapy
o.fb: That comparison belongs to the Kellner continuation ECT study.

o.t: ABFT versus enhanced usual care for suicidal adolescents
o.fb: That describes Diamond's ABFT trial.

o.t: ACT versus short-term hospitalization
o.fb: That describes Stein and Test's community-treatment study.

questions.q: Which result best captures why the Leff trial is memorable?

o.t: Couple therapy was a viable treatment and showed advantages on depressive outcomes and acceptability in this relationally selected group.
o.fb: The trial supports couple therapy when depression is embedded in critical partner relationships.

o.t: Antidepressants cured every participant and couple therapy had no role.
o.fb: The study did not show universal medication cure and supported couple therapy as clinically meaningful.

o.t: The trial proved that depression is always caused by marital conflict.
o.fb: The trial studied a selected relational context and should not be generalized as a single-cause model.

o.t: Both treatments were abandoned because neither improved symptoms.
o.fb: The study found improvement, with couple therapy showing important advantages.

questions.q: A patient with depression reports frequent criticism from a spouse but no intimate partner violence. What treatment implication follows from Leff 2000?

o.t: Assess whether couple therapy could address relationship processes maintaining depression.
o.fb: The trial supports considering couple therapy when partner criticism is clinically relevant.

o.t: Avoid asking about the relationship because depression treatment should be individual only.
o.fb: Relationship context can be central to assessment and treatment planning.

o.t: Use couple therapy even when there is active coercive violence and safety risk.
o.fb: Safety concerns such as intimate partner violence require specialized assessment and may contraindicate conjoint therapy.

o.t: Stop all antidepressants before discussing psychosocial options.
o.fb: Psychotherapy consideration does not require abrupt medication discontinuation.

questions.q: Which broader psychiatry concept does Leff 2000 illustrate?

o.t: Psychiatric symptoms can be treated by targeting interpersonal environments as well as individual symptoms.
o.fb: The trial is a clear example of relational treatment for an individual psychiatric disorder.

o.t: Only medication trials can provide evidence in psychiatry.
o.fb: This was a psychotherapy trial with clinically relevant outcomes.

o.t: Depression treatment should ignore relapse prevention.
o.fb: The study included treatment and maintenance considerations.

o.t: Partner criticism is useful because it motivates recovery.
o.fb: Criticism is a risk context, not a therapeutic tool.

questions.q: Pharoah 2010 is best described as which type of evidence?

o.t: A Cochrane systematic review of family interventions for schizophrenia
o.fb: It synthesized randomized evidence on family intervention rather than reporting a single new family-treatment site.

o.t: A single case report of psychodynamic therapy
o.fb: The Cochrane review synthesized multiple studies.

o.t: A genetic study of serotonin transporter alleles
o.fb: That is the Caspi gene-environment literature, not Pharoah's family-intervention review.

o.t: A diagnostic-validity proposal for psychiatric nosology
o.fb: Diagnostic validity is not the focus of this Cochrane family-intervention review.

questions.q: Which outcome did the Pharoah review find family interventions may improve in schizophrenia?

o.t: Relapse and hospitalization risk
o.fb: The review concluded that family intervention may reduce relapse events and hospitalizations.

o.t: A cure of schizophrenia after one session
o.fb: The evidence supports risk reduction, not cure.

o.t: Elimination of the need for antipsychotic medication in all patients
o.fb: Family intervention is an adjunctive psychosocial approach, not a universal medication replacement.

o.t: Immediate reversal of all negative symptoms
o.fb: The review does not support an immediate universal reversal of negative symptoms.

questions.q: What intervention content best matches family psychoeducation reviewed by Pharoah and colleagues?

o.t: Education, communication training, problem-solving, and relapse planning with family members
o.fb: These are common active components of structured family interventions.

o.t: A one-time instruction to relatives to monitor the patient silently
o.fb: Effective family interventions are structured and interactive rather than silent monitoring.

o.t: Unsupervised confrontation of psychotic beliefs by relatives
o.fb: Confrontational arguing is not the evidence-based family intervention strategy.

o.t: A medication algorithm with no family contact
o.fb: The review specifically concerns family psychosocial interventions.

questions.q: Which statement is the best evidence-based counseling point after the Pharoah review?

o.t: Family intervention can be offered as part of comprehensive schizophrenia care when relatives are involved.
o.fb: The review supports family intervention as an adjunct to comprehensive care.

o.t: Family intervention should replace medication and case management.
o.fb: The evidence does not support replacing other indicated treatments.

o.t: Family intervention is useful only if the family caused the illness.
o.fb: The intervention targets relapse risk and support, not blame.

o.t: Family intervention is contraindicated whenever schizophrenia is diagnosed.
o.fb: Schizophrenia is the condition for which the family-intervention evidence applies.

questions.q: Why is a Cochrane review especially useful for teaching this topic?

o.t: It summarizes patterns across trials, helping students separate a robust treatment theme from one isolated study.
o.fb: Systematic reviews are useful for seeing whether findings replicate across settings.

o.t: It removes the need to consider study quality.
o.fb: Cochrane reviews explicitly assess quality and limitations.

o.t: It proves every family intervention has the same effect size.
o.fb: Family interventions vary in content, dose, and study quality.

o.t: It is less reliable than a single anecdote.
o.fb: A systematic review generally provides stronger evidence than anecdote.

questions.q: Bateman and Fonagy's 1999 trial studied a structured treatment program for which condition?

o.t: Borderline personality disorder
o.fb: The trial randomized patients with borderline personality disorder to partial hospitalization or standard care.

o.t: Acute alcohol withdrawal
o.fb: The study was not an addiction detoxification trial.

o.t: Panic disorder treated with imipramine
o.fb: That population belongs to panic-disorder treatment research, not Bateman and Fonagy.

o.t: Major neurocognitive disorder treated with memantine
o.fb: The trial did not study dementia pharmacotherapy.

questions.q: Which intervention did Bateman 1999 evaluate?

o.t: Psychoanalytically oriented partial hospitalization including individual and group psychotherapy
o.fb: This structured day-treatment model became foundational for mentalization-based treatment.

o.t: A brief medication-only visit every six months
o.fb: The active treatment was intensive and psychotherapeutic, not medication-only.

o.t: A single family psychoeducation class for schizophrenia
o.fb: That resembles family-intervention literature, not this BPD partial-hospitalization study.

o.t: A diagnostic interview without treatment
o.fb: The study tested treatment outcomes rather than diagnostic assessment alone.

questions.q: Which outcome domain was central in Bateman 1999?

o.t: Suicidal and self-harming behavior, hospital use, and symptom distress
o.fb: The study assessed clinically meaningful BPD outcomes including self-harm and inpatient use.

o.t: Only cholesterol levels after antipsychotic exposure
o.fb: Metabolic monitoring was not the central outcome of this psychotherapy trial.

o.t: Only diagnostic validity of schizophrenia
o.fb: The trial examined treatment outcomes for BPD.

o.t: Only serum lithium level
o.fb: Lithium monitoring was not the primary outcome domain.

questions.q: What does mentalization-based treatment aim to strengthen?

o.t: The capacity to understand one's own and others' mental states, especially under attachment stress
o.fb: Mentalization is the ability to make sense of behavior in terms of thoughts, feelings, and intentions.

o.t: The ability to suppress all emotional discussion in therapy
o.fb: MBT explores mental states rather than suppressing emotional communication.

o.t: The capacity to memorize DSM codes without clinical formulation
o.fb: MBT is a treatment model, not a diagnostic memorization exercise.

o.t: The ability to avoid all interpersonal relationships
o.fb: MBT works directly with interpersonal understanding rather than avoidance.

questions.q: Which teaching point best follows from Bateman 1999?

o.t: Structured psychotherapy programs can meaningfully improve outcomes in BPD.
o.fb: The trial countered the view that BPD is untreatable or only manageable with crisis care.

o.t: BPD should be treated only with benzodiazepines.
o.fb: Psychotherapy is central to evidence-based BPD treatment; benzodiazepines can be risky.

o.t: Self-harm outcomes should be ignored in BPD trials.
o.fb: Self-harm and suicidality are key outcome domains.

o.t: Partial hospitalization is identical to no treatment.
o.fb: The structured partial-hospital program was the active intervention.

questions.q: Wampold's common-factors argument most directly challenges which overly narrow view of psychotherapy?

o.t: That outcomes are explained only by specific manualized techniques and not by relational or contextual factors
o.fb: The common-factors model emphasizes alliance, expectations, rationale, and therapist effects.

o.t: That psychotherapy requires a trained clinician
o.fb: The common-factors argument does not claim training is irrelevant.

o.t: That patients should be treated with empathy
o.fb: Empathy and alliance are part of what the common-factors literature highlights.

o.t: That treatment should be ethically delivered
o.fb: Ethical care is not what the common-factors argument challenges.

questions.q: Which factor is a classic common factor across bona fide psychotherapies?

o.t: A credible treatment rationale shared by patient and therapist
o.fb: A believable rationale can build hope, engagement, and therapeutic action across modalities.

o.t: The same homework worksheet for every diagnosis
o.fb: Common factors are not identical worksheets or identical techniques.

o.t: Avoiding discussion of treatment goals
o.fb: Goal agreement is often considered part of a strong therapeutic alliance.

o.t: A rule that the therapist must never adapt to the patient
o.fb: Responsiveness to the patient is clinically important and compatible with common-factors thinking.

questions.q: Which statement best avoids overclaiming Wampold's thesis?

o.t: Common factors matter substantially, but competent technique and fit to the clinical problem still matter.
o.fb: The useful teaching point is balance, not the claim that technique is meaningless.

o.t: All therapies are identical and training is unnecessary.
o.fb: The common-factors literature does not justify abandoning competence or training.

o.t: Only medication has specific treatment effects.
o.fb: Psychotherapies can have both shared and model-specific therapeutic processes.

o.t: Therapeutic alliance should not be measured.
o.fb: Alliance is a key process to monitor in psychotherapy.

questions.q: A student observes that two different evidence-based therapies can both help depression. Which Wampold-informed explanation is most appropriate?

o.t: Different bona fide therapies may share healing ingredients such as alliance, hope, structure, and emotional engagement.
o.fb: This is the core common-factors explanation for similar outcomes across credible therapies.

o.t: One of the studies must be fraudulent because only one therapy can work.
o.fb: Multiple therapies can be effective through overlapping and distinct mechanisms.

o.t: Depression outcomes cannot be measured in psychotherapy research.
o.fb: Depression outcomes are routinely measured in psychotherapy trials.

o.t: The result proves diagnosis is irrelevant to every treatment decision.
o.fb: Diagnosis and formulation still inform treatment matching and safety planning.

questions.q: Which MS3 behavior best applies the common-factors literature during a therapy observation?

o.t: Notice whether the patient and clinician share goals, trust, and a plausible treatment explanation.
o.fb: These alliance and expectancy elements are clinically meaningful across therapy models.

o.t: Judge the session only by whether a named manual page was followed exactly.
o.fb: Technique matters, but common factors require attention to relationship and shared meaning.

o.t: Ignore patient engagement because only diagnosis matters.
o.fb: Engagement is central to psychotherapy outcome.

o.t: Assume that warmth alone is sufficient for all high-risk patients.
o.fb: A good relationship is important but does not replace risk management or appropriate treatment structure.

questions.q: What was Shedler's main argument in the 2010 review of psychodynamic psychotherapy?

o.t: Empirical evidence supports psychodynamic therapy, with effects comparable to other evidence-based therapies.
o.fb: The review challenged the perception that psychodynamic therapy lacks evidence.

o.t: Psychodynamic therapy has never been studied empirically.
o.fb: Shedler reviewed empirical studies and meta-analytic findings.

o.t: Psychodynamic therapy is useful only as a placebo control.
o.fb: The review argued for real therapeutic efficacy.

o.t: Psychodynamic therapy should replace all acute safety interventions.
o.fb: Psychodynamic therapy evidence does not remove the need for safety assessment and crisis care.

questions.q: Which feature is commonly associated with psychodynamic psychotherapy?

o.t: Exploring affect, avoidance, recurring relationship patterns, and the therapeutic relationship
o.fb: These are core psychodynamic treatment processes described in the evidence base.

o.t: Focusing only on medication blood levels
o.fb: Medication monitoring is not a psychodynamic psychotherapy process.

o.t: Avoiding discussion of emotions to prevent transference
o.fb: Psychodynamic therapy often uses emotion and transference as treatment material.

o.t: Teaching families schizophrenia relapse-prevention scripts only
o.fb: That belongs to family psychoeducation rather than psychodynamic psychotherapy.

questions.q: Which finding from Shedler's review is especially useful for teaching?

o.t: Patients may maintain gains and continue improving after psychodynamic therapy ends.
o.fb: Shedler highlighted durable and sometimes continuing post-treatment gains.

o.t: Benefits disappear immediately after the last session in all studies.
o.fb: The review argued the opposite: gains can be maintained or increase.

o.t: Psychodynamic therapy works only by prescribing antidepressants.
o.fb: The review addressed psychotherapy effects, not medication prescribing.

o.t: Only inpatient psychodynamic therapy has ever been studied.
o.fb: Psychodynamic therapy has been studied in multiple formats and settings.

questions.q: A student says psychodynamic therapy is not evidence-based because it is older than CBT. What is the best correction?

o.t: Age of a therapy model does not determine evidence; psychodynamic therapy has empirical support.
o.fb: Shedler's review directly addresses the evidence misconception.

o.t: Older therapies are always superior to newer therapies.
o.fb: The point is evidence quality, not chronological superiority.

o.t: Evidence-based practice excludes psychotherapy research.
o.fb: Psychotherapy trials and meta-analyses are part of evidence-based practice.

o.t: CBT has no evidence for any disorder.
o.fb: CBT has a strong evidence base; the correction is that psychodynamic therapy also has evidence.

questions.q: Which clinical scenario is a reasonable place to consider psychodynamic formulation?

o.t: A patient with recurring interpersonal conflicts and affective patterns that repeat across settings
o.fb: Psychodynamic formulation is especially suited to recurring relational and emotional patterns.

o.t: A patient with septic shock needing immediate antibiotics
o.fb: Acute medical stabilization takes priority in that setting.

o.t: A patient refusing capacity assessment because psychodynamics replaces consent law
o.fb: Psychodynamic formulation does not replace capacity assessment.

o.t: A patient requesting a genetic test for complement C4 risk
o.fb: That request relates to genetics, not psychodynamic treatment selection.

questions.q: According to Appelbaum's framework, which ability is required for treatment decision-making capacity?

o.t: Communicating a stable choice about the proposed treatment
o.fb: Communicating a choice is one of the four core abilities in capacity assessment.

o.t: Having a psychiatric diagnosis
o.fb: Diagnosis alone does not determine capacity.

o.t: Agreeing with the physician's recommendation
o.fb: A patient can have capacity and still refuse recommended treatment.

o.t: Scoring above average on an IQ test
o.fb: Capacity is decision-specific and not reducible to IQ.

questions.q: Which list best matches the four abilities model of capacity?

o.t: Choice, understanding, appreciation, and reasoning
o.fb: These four abilities organize modern clinical capacity assessment.

o.t: Mood, sleep, appetite, and energy
o.fb: Those are depressive symptom domains, not the capacity abilities.

o.t: Insight, hallucinations, delusions, and affect
o.fb: Psychotic symptoms may affect capacity but are not the four-abilities checklist.

o.t: Risk, resources, relatives, and religion
o.fb: Those may be contextual factors but are not Appelbaum's four abilities.

questions.q: A patient can repeat the facts of surgery but denies that the diagnosis applies to him because the lab results were planted by aliens. Which capacity ability is most impaired?

o.t: Appreciation
o.fb: Appreciation is the ability to apply relevant information to one's own situation and consequences.

o.t: Visual acuity
o.fb: The problem is not seeing the information but applying it realistically to himself.

o.t: Motor coordination
o.fb: Motor function is not the impaired capacity domain in this vignette.

o.t: Expressed emotion
o.fb: Expressed emotion is a family-relapse construct, not a capacity ability.

questions.q: Which statement about capacity is most accurate?

o.t: Capacity is task-specific and may fluctuate over time.
o.fb: A patient may have capacity for one decision but not another, and capacity can change.

o.t: Capacity is absent in every patient admitted involuntarily.
o.fb: Involuntary status does not automatically remove capacity for all treatment decisions.

o.t: Capacity can be determined only by whether the patient agrees with treatment.
o.fb: Agreement is not the standard; the decision-making process is.

o.t: Capacity never improves after delirium or psychosis is treated.
o.fb: Treating reversible impairments can restore capacity.

questions.q: What is the clinician's role when decision-making capacity is uncertain?

o.t: Assess and document the relevant abilities, maximize the patient's functioning, and seek legal adjudication when needed.
o.fb: Appelbaum emphasizes careful clinical assessment while recognizing that formal incompetence is a legal determination.

o.t: Declare the patient legally incompetent without documentation.
o.fb: Legal incompetence is not declared casually by undocumented clinical impression.

o.t: Ignore the patient's reasoning if the family disagrees.
o.fb: Family input may help, but the patient's decision-making abilities must be assessed.

o.t: Avoid explaining the treatment because capacity is already fixed.
o.fb: Providing information and support can improve the patient's ability to decide.

questions.q: The McLean Study of Adult Development is most important because it changed assumptions about which aspect of borderline personality disorder?

o.t: Longitudinal course and likelihood of remission
o.fb: The study showed that symptomatic remission in BPD is far more common than earlier pessimistic views suggested.

o.t: The acute efficacy of antipsychotics for schizophrenia
o.fb: That is a different clinical area and study tradition.

o.t: The genetic basis of complement activation
o.fb: Complement genetics is unrelated to the MSAD BPD follow-up study.

o.t: The diagnosis of delirium in mechanically ventilated patients
o.fb: The MSAD followed adults with borderline personality disorder, not ICU delirium.

questions.q: Which finding best reflects Zanarini's early MSAD follow-up?

o.t: Many patients with BPD achieved remission, and recurrences were less common than expected.
o.fb: The study provided a more hopeful and empirically grounded prognosis for BPD.

o.t: BPD symptoms never remit once diagnosed.
o.fb: The MSAD directly challenged this pessimistic belief.

o.t: Completed suicide occurred in most patients during follow-up.
o.fb: Suicide risk remains serious, but the observed rate was lower than older assumptions.

o.t: Medication alone produced immediate functional recovery in all participants.
o.fb: The study was longitudinal and did not show universal medication-only recovery.

questions.q: Which symptom-course distinction is associated with Zanarini's BPD work?

o.t: Some acute symptoms improve sooner, while temperamental and interpersonal features may persist longer.
o.fb: The course of BPD is heterogeneous, with different symptom domains changing at different rates.

o.t: All BPD symptoms improve at the same speed in every patient.
o.fb: The MSAD emphasized differential symptom-course patterns.

o.t: Only hallucinations define BPD prognosis.
o.fb: Hallucinations are not the central prognostic marker in BPD course studies.

o.t: BPD course can be predicted perfectly at intake.
o.fb: Longitudinal outcomes are variable and cannot be predicted perfectly.

questions.q: A patient with new BPD diagnosis asks if improvement is possible. Which answer best reflects Zanarini 2005?

o.t: Yes; many patients improve substantially over time, though functional recovery may require sustained treatment and support.
o.fb: The study supports realistic hope while recognizing ongoing functional challenges.

o.t: No; remission is essentially impossible.
o.fb: That contradicts the longitudinal findings.

o.t: Yes; symptoms always disappear within one week of diagnosis.
o.fb: Improvement is possible but usually not instantaneous or uniform.

o.t: Only inpatient admission can produce remission.
o.fb: BPD improvement is not limited to inpatient treatment.

questions.q: What is a key clinical implication of the MSAD findings for stigma reduction?

o.t: Clinicians should avoid describing BPD as untreatable or hopeless.
o.fb: The longitudinal evidence supports a hopeful, evidence-based stance.

o.t: Clinicians should avoid offering psychotherapy because patients remit automatically.
o.fb: Hopeful prognosis does not remove the need for evidence-based care.

o.t: Clinicians should use BPD diagnosis only as an exclusion criterion.
o.fb: The diagnosis should guide treatment and support, not exclusion.

o.t: Clinicians should assume self-harm is never clinically serious in BPD.
o.fb: Self-harm and suicide risk must always be taken seriously.

questions.q: Which feature is central to borderline personality disorder as summarized in Gunderson's review?

o.t: Extreme sensitivity to perceived interpersonal slights with unstable self-image and affective volatility
o.fb: Interpersonal hypersensitivity, identity disturbance, affective instability, and impulsivity are core BPD features.

o.t: Progressive memory loss as the defining symptom
o.fb: Progressive memory loss suggests a neurocognitive disorder rather than BPD.

o.t: Fixed negative symptoms without interpersonal reactivity
o.fb: Negative symptoms are more characteristic of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.

o.t: Only panic attacks triggered by public places
o.fb: That pattern would point toward anxiety disorders, not BPD.

questions.q: Which treatment statement best reflects Gunderson 2018?

o.t: Evidence-based psychotherapy is central; medication is usually adjunctive and symptom-targeted.
o.fb: The review emphasizes psychosocial treatment rather than medication as a cure for core BPD.

o.t: BPD is treated primarily with indefinite benzodiazepines.
o.fb: Benzodiazepines can worsen disinhibition and are not first-line BPD treatment.

o.t: No psychotherapy has any role in BPD.
o.fb: Multiple structured psychotherapies have evidence for BPD.

o.t: Medication eliminates the need for a therapeutic frame.
o.fb: A consistent therapeutic frame is important in BPD care.

questions.q: A student says patients with BPD are manipulative and cannot improve. What is the best evidence-based response?

o.t: BPD involves severe emotion and relationship dysregulation, and many patients improve with structured treatment.
o.fb: This replaces stigma with a clinically accurate and hopeful formulation.

o.t: The statement is correct, so treatment should be withheld.
o.fb: Withholding care based on stigma is inappropriate and unsupported.

o.t: BPD symptoms are always intentional and never associated with distress.
o.fb: BPD symptoms are associated with substantial distress and risk.

o.t: BPD is only a legal term and not a clinical diagnosis.
o.fb: BPD is a clinical diagnosis with an evidence base.

questions.q: Which clinical stance is most useful when caring for patients with BPD?

o.t: Validate distress, maintain clear boundaries, and use a structured treatment plan.
o.fb: BPD care benefits from both empathy and consistency.

o.t: Avoid boundaries because any limit-setting is harmful.
o.fb: Clear, compassionate boundaries are often therapeutic.

o.t: Respond to every crisis with a different plan to show flexibility.
o.fb: Inconsistent plans can worsen instability; structure matters.

o.t: Exclude the patient from psychotherapy if self-harm is present.
o.fb: Self-harm is a common treatment target in evidence-based BPD psychotherapies.

questions.q: What prognostic message is most consistent with Gunderson 2018?

o.t: Symptomatic remission is common over time, though social and vocational recovery may lag.
o.fb: Modern BPD reviews emphasize both hope for symptom improvement and the need to address functioning.

o.t: BPD inevitably worsens in every patient.
o.fb: That pessimistic view is inconsistent with longitudinal evidence.

o.t: BPD disappears after one medication dose.
o.fb: Improvement usually requires sustained treatment and time.

o.t: BPD has no relationship to suicide risk.
o.fb: Suicide risk and self-harm require careful assessment in BPD.

questions.q: Franklin 2017 reviewed 50 years of research on which clinical problem?

o.t: Longitudinal prediction of suicidal thoughts and behaviors
o.fb: The meta-analysis examined risk factors for future suicidal thoughts and behaviors.

o.t: Acute efficacy of antidepressants in adult depression
o.fb: The paper focused on suicide-risk prediction, not antidepressant efficacy.

o.t: Medication titration in pediatric ADHD
o.fb: That topic belongs to the MTA ADHD study.

o.t: Family psychoeducation for schizophrenia relapse
o.fb: That topic belongs to the family-intervention literature.

questions.q: What was the most important finding of the Franklin meta-analysis for clinical risk assessment?

o.t: Traditional risk factors predicted suicidal outcomes only modestly, often only slightly better than chance.
o.fb: The paper warned against overconfidence in individual-level prediction.

o.t: One risk factor perfectly predicted suicide in all settings.
o.fb: No broad risk-factor category provided near-perfect prediction.

o.t: Risk factors were irrelevant because suicide cannot be studied.
o.fb: Risk factors matter, but their predictive power is limited.

o.t: Prediction accuracy has improved dramatically without new methods.
o.fb: The review found that prediction had not substantially improved across decades.

questions.q: Which clinical implication follows from Franklin 2017?

o.t: Use risk factors to inform formulation, but do not rely on them as precise individual prediction tools.
o.fb: Risk assessment should guide care while acknowledging prediction limits.

o.t: Stop asking about suicide risk because prediction is imperfect.
o.fb: Imperfect prediction does not eliminate the need for assessment and intervention.

o.t: Use a simple high-risk label as the complete treatment plan.
o.fb: Risk labels should not substitute for safety planning and treatment.

o.t: Discharge all patients with no static risk factors without follow-up.
o.fb: Absence of known risk factors does not guarantee safety.

questions.q: A student asks why safety planning matters if risk prediction is weak. What is the best answer?

o.t: Because prevention should focus on actionable supports and means safety, not only on predicting who will die by suicide.
o.fb: Franklin's findings support shifting from prediction overconfidence toward practical prevention.

o.t: Safety planning matters only when a scale produces a perfect score.
o.fb: Safety planning is useful precisely because prediction is imperfect.

o.t: Safety planning is contraindicated when risk factors are present.
o.fb: Risk factors increase the need for safety planning.

o.t: Safety planning is only a research tool and not clinical care.
o.fb: Safety planning is a clinical intervention used in suicide prevention.

questions.q: Which research direction is most responsive to Franklin 2017?

o.t: Developing stronger, prospective, multivariable and near-term prediction models while testing interventions
o.fb: The review suggests the field needs better methods and more intervention-focused work.

o.t: Repeating only small cross-sectional studies of one risk factor
o.fb: The meta-analysis showed limits of the traditional isolated-risk-factor approach.

o.t: Avoiding prospective follow-up because it is too informative
o.fb: Prospective follow-up is essential for prediction research.

o.t: Assuming old risk-factor lists are already sufficient
o.fb: The review challenged that assumption.

questions.q: Caspi 2003 is famous for proposing what kind of relationship between life stress and depression?

o.t: A gene-by-environment interaction involving 5-HTTLPR and stressful life events
o.fb: The study proposed that serotonin transporter promoter variation moderated the depression risk associated with stress.

o.t: A randomized medication effect of SSRIs on childhood trauma
o.fb: The study was observational and did not randomize antidepressant treatment.

o.t: A family psychoeducation effect on schizophrenia relapse
o.fb: That is a separate psychosocial schizophrenia literature.

o.t: A diagnostic-validity framework for schizophrenia
o.fb: Robins and Guze, not Caspi, proposed the classic diagnostic-validity framework.

questions.q: In the original Caspi report, which genotype pattern was associated with greater stress-related depression vulnerability?

o.t: One or two copies of the short allele
o.fb: The reported interaction suggested that short-allele carriers had more depressive outcomes after stress.

o.t: Two copies of a complement C4A high-expression allele
o.fb: Complement C4A belongs to schizophrenia genetics, not the 5-HTTLPR depression study.

o.t: A mutation that directly causes BPD in all carriers
o.fb: The study was about moderated stress response, not a deterministic BPD mutation.

o.t: Absence of any measured genetic variation
o.fb: The paper specifically examined serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism.

questions.q: Which design feature is important for interpreting Caspi 2003?

o.t: It used a prospective longitudinal birth cohort rather than a randomized trial.
o.fb: The design supports temporal observation but does not randomize genes or life stress.

o.t: It randomly assigned participants to stressful life events.
o.fb: Stressful life events were observed, not assigned.

o.t: It enrolled only inpatients receiving ECT.
o.fb: The study was a population cohort, not an ECT trial.

o.t: It was a Cochrane review of family therapy.
o.fb: Caspi 2003 was an original cohort study, not a systematic review.

questions.q: What was the broader influence of Caspi 2003?

o.t: It accelerated interest in gene-environment interactions in psychiatric disorders.
o.fb: The paper became a landmark example of biological vulnerability interacting with environmental stress.

o.t: It established 5-HTTLPR testing as a standard clinical depression test.
o.fb: The finding did not become a recommended clinical genetic test.

o.t: It proved depression is caused only by serotonin deficiency.
o.fb: The study focused on moderation of stress risk, not a simple serotonin-deficiency model.

o.t: It eliminated the need to ask about psychosocial stress.
o.fb: Stress exposure was central to the proposed interaction.

questions.q: Which clinical use of Caspi 2003 would be inappropriate today?

o.t: Ordering 5-HTTLPR testing to decide whether a patient will become depressed after stress
o.fb: The finding is historically important but not a clinically validated individual prediction test.

o.t: Using the study to teach the concept of gene-environment interaction
o.fb: The study remains useful pedagogically for explaining gene-environment hypotheses.

o.t: Discussing how stress and vulnerability can interact
o.fb: That is an appropriate conceptual use.

o.t: Comparing the original finding with later replication attempts
o.fb: The study is often taught alongside later non-replication literature.

questions.q: Border 2019 primarily challenged which area of depression genetics?

o.t: Historical candidate gene and candidate gene-by-environment hypotheses
o.fb: The study tested widely studied candidate genes and found no support across large samples.

o.t: The efficacy of family psychoeducation for schizophrenia
o.fb: Border 2019 was a genetics study, not a family-intervention trial.

o.t: The diagnosis of borderline personality disorder
o.fb: The study focused on depression genetics, not BPD diagnosis.

o.t: The use of ECT after depression remission
o.fb: ECT continuation was not the subject of Border 2019.

questions.q: Which methodological feature made Border 2019 more persuasive than many earlier candidate gene studies?

o.t: Very large samples and preregistered analyses across multiple depression phenotypes
o.fb: Large, preregistered analyses reduce false-positive risk compared with small exploratory studies.

o.t: A single uncontrolled case report
o.fb: The study's strength was scale and systematic analysis, not anecdote.

o.t: Random assignment to different genotypes
o.fb: Genotypes cannot be randomized in this kind of human genetic study.

o.t: Excluding environmental measures entirely from every analysis
o.fb: The paper explicitly examined candidate gene and gene-by-environment hypotheses.

questions.q: What did Border 2019 imply about 5-HTTLPR depression-risk claims?

o.t: They should not be treated as established clinical predictors of depression.
o.fb: The study found no support for historical candidate gene hypotheses at clinical-prediction strength.

o.t: They are now definitive enough for routine clinical testing.
o.fb: The study argues against that conclusion.

o.t: They prove that environment has no role in depression.
o.fb: Non-replication of specific candidate-gene claims does not erase environmental risk.

o.t: They show that all genetic research in psychiatry is impossible.
o.fb: The paper critiques candidate gene approaches, not all psychiatric genetics.

questions.q: How should students reconcile Caspi 2003 and Border 2019?

o.t: Caspi is historically important and hypothesis-generating; Border shows the need for adequately powered replication.
o.fb: This teaches scientific self-correction rather than simple dismissal of either paper.

o.t: Caspi proves clinical testing is mandatory despite later evidence.
o.fb: Later non-replication cautions against clinical testing.

o.t: Border proves life stress never affects depression.
o.fb: Border addressed candidate gene hypotheses, not whether stress matters.

o.t: The two studies are unrelated because neither discusses genes.
o.fb: Both are central to teaching candidate gene and gene-environment claims.

questions.q: Which research practice is most reinforced by Border 2019?

o.t: Preregistration, large samples, and replication before clinical translation
o.fb: The study is a clear example of why robust methods matter in psychiatric genetics.

o.t: Publishing small positive findings without replication as clinical tests
o.fb: That is exactly the kind of premature translation the paper cautions against.

o.t: Avoiding transparent analytic plans
o.fb: Transparency strengthens credibility.

o.t: Using candidate genes as deterministic explanations for complex disorders
o.fb: Complex psychiatric disorders are not explained by single deterministic candidate genes.

questions.q: Sekar 2016 investigated the strongest common genetic association for schizophrenia in which genomic region?

o.t: The major histocompatibility complex region involving complement component 4
o.fb: The study helped explain part of the MHC association through structural variation in C4.

o.t: The serotonin transporter promoter as a depression-only locus
o.fb: 5-HTTLPR is associated with the Caspi depression literature, not Sekar's C4 schizophrenia study.

o.t: The dopamine transporter gene in ADHD treatment response
o.fb: Sekar 2016 focused on schizophrenia risk and complement biology.

o.t: A mitochondrial mutation causing all psychotic disorders
o.fb: The study did not identify a single deterministic mitochondrial cause.

questions.q: Which C4-related finding was most central to the Sekar paper?

o.t: C4 alleles associated with higher C4A expression were linked to greater schizophrenia risk.
o.fb: The paper connected structural C4 variation, C4A expression, and schizophrenia risk.

o.t: Low C4A expression fully protected every carrier from schizophrenia.
o.fb: The association was probabilistic, not fully protective or deterministic.

o.t: C4 had no expression in the brain.
o.fb: The study found complement-related expression and localization relevant to brain biology.

o.t: C4 variation explained all schizophrenia heritability.
o.fb: C4 explains only part of a complex polygenic risk architecture.

questions.q: What neurodevelopmental mechanism did Sekar 2016 help connect to schizophrenia risk?

o.t: Complement-mediated synaptic pruning
o.fb: The paper linked complement biology to synapse elimination, a plausible neurodevelopmental mechanism.

o.t: Direct serotonin depletion as the sole cause of psychosis
o.fb: The study did not support a simple serotonin-depletion model.

o.t: Antidepressant withdrawal from SSRIs
o.fb: Withdrawal is unrelated to the C4 schizophrenia genetics mechanism.

o.t: Family criticism as a genetic mutation
o.fb: Family expressed emotion is a psychosocial relapse factor, not a genetic mutation.

questions.q: Which clinical statement about C4 testing is most appropriate?

o.t: C4 findings are mechanistically important but not a stand-alone diagnostic test for schizophrenia.
o.fb: The association improves biological understanding but is not clinically deterministic.

o.t: C4 testing can diagnose schizophrenia in asymptomatic children.
o.fb: That overstates the clinical utility of the finding.

o.t: C4 status determines which antipsychotic will work for every patient.
o.fb: The study did not provide a medication-selection test.

o.t: C4 findings eliminate the need for psychosocial treatment.
o.fb: Biological mechanisms do not replace comprehensive care.

questions.q: Why is Sekar 2016 useful in a psychiatry clerkship curriculum?

o.t: It shows how genetic association can point toward a plausible brain mechanism.
o.fb: The study bridges population genetics, complement biology, and synaptic development.

o.t: It proves psychiatric disorders are not biological.
o.fb: The paper is an example of biologically grounded psychiatric research.

o.t: It shows that single genes determine complex psychiatric diagnoses.
o.fb: The finding is probabilistic within a polygenic disorder.

o.t: It replaces clinical interviewing with whole-genome sequencing.
o.fb: Clinical diagnosis still relies on clinical assessment.

questions.q: Kernberg's personality organization model is most useful for assessing which structural features?

o.t: Identity integration, predominant defenses, and reality testing
o.fb: These domains help distinguish neurotic, borderline, and psychotic levels of personality organization.

o.t: Serum lithium level, creatinine, and thyroid function
o.fb: Those labs matter for lithium monitoring, not personality organization.

o.t: C4A copy number alone
o.fb: C4 genetics is unrelated to Kernberg's structural clinical interview model.

o.t: Forced expiratory volume and oxygen saturation
o.fb: Pulmonary measures are not the structural domains of personality organization.

questions.q: In Kernberg's model, borderline personality organization is classically associated with which pattern?

o.t: Identity diffusion, primitive defenses, and generally intact reality testing
o.fb: This combination distinguishes borderline organization from psychotic organization.

o.t: Fully integrated identity, mature defenses, and no interpersonal conflict
o.fb: That description is closer to healthier or neurotic-level functioning.

o.t: Permanent loss of reality testing in every interaction
o.fb: Persistent loss of reality testing would suggest psychotic-level organization.

o.t: Absence of any defenses or affective reactions
o.fb: Defensive style and affective reactivity are central to the model.

questions.q: Which defense is most associated with borderline personality organization in Kernberg's framework?

o.t: Splitting
o.fb: Splitting is a classic primitive defense emphasized in Kernberg's model.

o.t: Sublimation as the only defense
o.fb: Sublimation is a mature defense and not the hallmark primitive defense here.

o.t: No defensive processes
o.fb: The model explicitly evaluates defenses.

o.t: Bronchodilation
o.fb: Bronchodilation is a physiologic process, not a psychological defense.

questions.q: How should students distinguish borderline personality organization from DSM borderline personality disorder?

o.t: Personality organization is a structural formulation and is not identical to a DSM categorical diagnosis.
o.fb: Kernberg's model can inform formulation across diagnoses and is broader than DSM BPD.

o.t: They are exactly the same term in every clinical context.
o.fb: The structural model and DSM category overlap but are not identical.

o.t: Personality organization is a lab test and DSM BPD is a medication dose.
o.fb: Both are clinical concepts, but one is a structural formulation and one is a diagnostic category.

o.t: DSM BPD is diagnosed only by C4A expression.
o.fb: DSM BPD is diagnosed clinically, not by complement genetics.

questions.q: What is the practical value of Kernberg's model in psychotherapy planning?

o.t: It helps anticipate transference, defenses, identity disturbance, and level of structure needed in treatment.
o.fb: Structural formulation guides therapeutic stance and treatment frame.

o.t: It determines the exact antidepressant dose for every patient.
o.fb: The model is psychodynamic and structural, not a dosing algorithm.

o.t: It eliminates the need for risk assessment.
o.fb: Risk assessment remains essential regardless of formulation.

o.t: It proves psychotherapy cannot help personality pathology.
o.fb: Kernberg's work is closely tied to psychotherapy for severe personality pathology.

questions.q: Gabbard's boundary paper is most useful for teaching which clinical distinction?

o.t: Boundary crossings may be benign or clinically justified, while boundary violations exploit or harm the patient.
o.fb: The paper emphasizes clinical context while distinguishing crossings from harmful violations.

o.t: All boundary crossings are identical to sexual misconduct.
o.fb: Some crossings can be clinically appropriate; violations are harmful or exploitative.

o.t: Boundaries are irrelevant if the clinician has good intentions.
o.fb: Good intentions do not remove the need for boundary awareness and risk management.
