o.t: Boundary issues occur only in inpatient units.
o.fb: Boundary issues can occur in any clinical setting.

questions.q: Which area is part of Gabbard's boundary framework?

o.t: Role, time, place, money, gifts, self-disclosure, language, and physical contact
o.fb: These are examples of clinical boundary domains reviewed in the paper.

o.t: Only medication dose and insurance formulary
o.fb: Medication and insurance matter clinically but do not capture the boundary framework.

o.t: Only whether the patient has capacity
o.fb: Capacity is a separate ethics topic from therapeutic boundaries.

o.t: Only whether the patient agrees with the clinician
o.fb: Agreement does not define whether boundaries are appropriate.

questions.q: Which behavior is best classified as a serious boundary violation?

o.t: A sexual relationship with a current patient
o.fb: Sexual contact with a current patient is exploitative and never clinically justified.

o.t: A brief, clinically relevant self-disclosure used to support treatment goals
o.fb: Limited self-disclosure can be a crossing that requires judgment, not automatically a violation.

o.t: Extending a session briefly during an acute safety crisis
o.fb: A time boundary crossing may be clinically justified depending on context.

o.t: Accepting a modest culturally meaningful token after discussing implications
o.fb: Gift situations require careful judgment and documentation rather than automatic classification as severe violation.

questions.q: A patient offers an expensive gift to a resident. Which response best reflects boundary-aware practice?

o.t: Explore the meaning of the gift, maintain the treatment frame, consult if needed, and document the decision.
o.fb: Boundary decisions should be clinically reasoned rather than impulsive.

o.t: Accept it immediately to avoid hurting the patient's feelings.
o.fb: Expensive gifts can create exploitation, obligation, or frame problems.

o.t: Shame the patient for making an inappropriate offer.
o.fb: A respectful exploration is preferable to shaming.

o.t: Ignore the event and do not document anything.
o.fb: Boundary issues should be addressed and documented when clinically relevant.

questions.q: What is the best risk-management lesson from Gabbard 1995?

o.t: Maintain a clear therapeutic frame and seek consultation when boundary decisions become ambiguous.
o.fb: Consultation and a consistent frame reduce risk and improve patient care.

o.t: Boundary problems are solved by avoiding empathy.
o.fb: Empathy is compatible with clear boundaries.

o.t: Any patient request requires automatic termination.
o.fb: Boundary concerns require assessment, not automatic termination.

o.t: Documentation is unnecessary if the clinician meant well.
o.fb: Documentation is part of thoughtful boundary management.

questions.q: Robins and Guze proposed which approach to establishing validity in psychiatric diagnosis?

o.t: Clinical description, laboratory studies, delimitation from other disorders, follow-up, and family studies
o.fb: These five phases became a classic framework for validating psychiatric diagnoses.

o.t: A single symptom checklist with no longitudinal or family data
o.fb: Their model explicitly goes beyond cross-sectional symptom description.

o.t: Only patient preference for a diagnosis
o.fb: Patient experience matters, but diagnostic validity requires multiple evidence domains.

o.t: Medication response as the only criterion
o.fb: Treatment response alone is not the full Robins-Guze framework.

questions.q: Which evidence domain is illustrated by showing that a syndrome has a characteristic long-term course?

o.t: Follow-up study
o.fb: Longitudinal course is part of the follow-up phase of diagnostic validation.

o.t: Gift boundary analysis
o.fb: Boundary analysis is an ethics topic, not diagnostic validity.

o.t: Medication discontinuation syndrome
o.fb: Withdrawal symptoms are not the diagnostic-validity evidence domain described here.

o.t: Transference interpretation
o.fb: Transference may matter in therapy but is not the follow-up validation phase.

questions.q: What does delimitation from other disorders mean in the Robins-Guze framework?

o.t: Showing that the syndrome can be distinguished from neighboring diagnostic conditions
o.fb: Delimitation asks whether boundaries between diagnoses are clinically and empirically defensible.

o.t: Avoiding all differential diagnosis
o.fb: Delimitation requires careful differential diagnosis.

o.t: Making diagnoses based only on family preference
o.fb: Family studies are one evidence domain, not the whole delimitation process.

o.t: Assuming all psychiatric diagnoses are identical
o.fb: The framework aims to distinguish valid syndromes.

questions.q: Why was the Robins-Guze paper important for modern psychiatric nosology?

o.t: It framed psychiatric diagnoses as hypotheses that should be tested against multiple validators.
o.fb: This helped move psychiatry toward operational, evidence-informed diagnostic categories.

o.t: It proved no psychiatric diagnosis can ever be valid.
o.fb: The paper proposed a method for evaluating validity, not abandoning diagnosis.

o.t: It replaced all diagnosis with psychotherapy technique.
o.fb: The paper is about nosology rather than treatment technique.

o.t: It argued that family history should never be collected.
o.fb: Family studies are one of the proposed validators.

questions.q: Which research finding would strengthen diagnostic validity under the Robins-Guze model?

o.t: A syndrome has a consistent clinical picture, family aggregation, and a distinguishable longitudinal course.
o.fb: That pattern addresses several validators in the framework.

o.t: A diagnosis is popular on social media for one month.
o.fb: Popularity does not establish diagnostic validity.

o.t: A clinician can remember the acronym easily.
o.fb: Mnemonic ease is not a validity criterion.

o.t: The syndrome has no boundaries, course, or family pattern.
o.fb: That would weaken rather than strengthen diagnostic validity.

questions.q: Stein and Test's community-treatment program is an early foundation for which service model?

o.t: Assertive Community Treatment
o.fb: The study helped establish intensive, team-based community care for people with severe mental illness.

o.t: Attachment-Based Family Therapy
o.fb: ABFT is a family therapy for suicidal adolescents, not Stein and Test's community psychiatry model.

o.t: Mentalization-Based Treatment
o.fb: MBT is a psychotherapy for BPD, not a community-treatment team model.

o.t: Research Domain Criteria
o.fb: RDoC is a research classification framework, not an ACT service model.

questions.q: Which feature best describes the Stein-Test model?

o.t: Comprehensive, ongoing, community-based services delivered by an active treatment team
o.fb: The model emphasized bringing services to patients in the community rather than relying only on clinic visits.

o.t: A brief advice session after discharge with no follow-up
o.fb: ACT is intensive and ongoing, not a one-time discharge instruction.

o.t: A genetics-only risk consultation
o.fb: The model addresses community functioning and service delivery.

o.t: A medication trial with placebo blinding
o.fb: The study evaluated a service model rather than a blinded medication trial.

questions.q: What outcome pattern made Stein-Test 1980 influential?

o.t: The community program reduced hospitalization and improved community tenure while it was active.
o.fb: The study showed that intensive community programming could reduce reliance on hospital care.

o.t: Hospital use increased sharply during the program and improved only after it stopped.
o.fb: The study found gains during active programming and deterioration after discontinuation.

o.t: A single office visit eliminated all functional impairment.
o.fb: The model required comprehensive ongoing services.

o.t: The program showed that community treatment is impossible.
o.fb: The study supported community treatment when services are intensive and sustained.

questions.q: Which patient is the best match for ACT-style services?

o.t: A person with severe mental illness, repeated hospitalizations, and difficulty engaging in office-based care
o.fb: ACT is designed for high-need patients who require outreach and comprehensive community support.

o.t: A healthy adult requesting a one-time work physical
o.fb: ACT is not intended for routine preventive care in low-need patients.

o.t: A patient with mild insomnia who wants sleep-hygiene handouts only
o.fb: ACT is too intensive for isolated mild insomnia.

o.t: A patient whose only need is a diagnostic-validity research interview
o.fb: ACT is a treatment service model, not only a research interview.

questions.q: What lesson follows from the deterioration seen after special programming was discontinued?

o.t: For many high-need patients, community supports must be durable rather than brief demonstration projects.
o.fb: The study suggested that ongoing comprehensive programming is needed to sustain gains.

o.t: ACT should always be stopped as soon as hospital use decreases.
o.fb: Stopping support may risk loss of gains.

o.t: Community care works only if no team is involved.
o.fb: The team-based model was central to the intervention.

o.t: Hospitalization is the only possible treatment for chronic mental illness.
o.fb: The program showed that community-based alternatives can work when adequately resourced.

questions.q: The ACE Study examined the relationship between childhood adversity and which later outcomes?

o.t: Adult health risk behaviors, health status, and disease
o.fb: The study linked categories of adverse childhood experiences with a broad range of adult health outcomes.

o.t: Only short-term antidepressant response
o.fb: The ACE Study was not an antidepressant treatment trial.

o.t: Only schizophrenia relapse after discharge
o.fb: Schizophrenia relapse is the focus of family-intervention studies, not the ACE Study.

o.t: Only inpatient length of stay after ECT
o.fb: The ACE Study examined long-term health associations after childhood adversity.

questions.q: Which exposure category was included in the original ACE framework?

o.t: Childhood abuse or household dysfunction such as substance abuse, mental illness, or incarceration in the home
o.fb: The study counted multiple categories of abuse and household dysfunction.

o.t: Only whether the child watched television
o.fb: Television viewing was not an original ACE exposure category.

o.t: Only adult occupational stress
o.fb: The ACE Study focused on childhood exposures.

o.t: Only genetic complement variation
o.fb: Complement variation is unrelated to the ACE exposure categories.

questions.q: What does the dose-response pattern in the ACE Study mean?

o.t: As the number of ACE categories increased, risk for multiple adverse adult outcomes increased.
o.fb: The graded association is one of the study's most important findings.

o.t: One specific ACE category perfectly predicted every adult disease.
o.fb: The study found graded risk, not perfect prediction.

o.t: Childhood adversity had no relation to adult health.
o.fb: The study found strong associations between adversity burden and adult outcomes.

o.t: Only protective childhood experiences mattered.
o.fb: The original ACE Study focused on adverse categories.

questions.q: Which clinical use of ACE information is most trauma-informed?

o.t: Ask sensitively when relevant, respond with validation and resources, and avoid forcing disclosure.
o.fb: Trauma-informed care emphasizes safety, choice, and support.

o.t: Use the ACE score to blame patients for adult illness.
o.fb: The ACE framework should reduce blame, not increase it.

o.t: Require detailed trauma disclosure at the first visit regardless of readiness.
o.fb: Forcing disclosure can be harmful and is not trauma-informed.

o.t: Treat the ACE score as a deterministic diagnosis.
o.fb: ACE burden indicates risk, not destiny.

questions.q: What is a key limitation when applying the ACE Study to individual patients?

o.t: Population-level risk associations do not determine an individual patient's future.
o.fb: ACE findings are powerful for public health but should not be used deterministically.

o.t: The study proves adversity has no biologic effects.
o.fb: The study is often used to teach long-term health effects of adversity.

o.t: The study included no adults.
o.fb: The original cohort included adult HMO members reporting childhood experiences.

o.t: The study was a randomized trial assigning children to adversity.
o.fb: The study was observational and did not assign adversity.

questions.q: Volkow 2016 presents addiction primarily as what kind of condition?

o.t: A chronic brain disease involving reward, stress, and self-control circuits
o.fb: The brain disease model emphasizes neuroadaptations that affect craving, control, and relapse risk.

o.t: A simple moral failure with no neurobiology
o.fb: The paper explicitly argues against a purely moralizing account.

o.t: A condition cured by one detoxification admission in all patients
o.fb: Addiction is often chronic and relapsing, requiring continuing care.

o.t: A diagnostic category unrelated to environment
o.fb: The model includes biological vulnerability while recognizing environmental and social influences.

questions.q: Which clinical feature is central to addiction in Volkow's model?

o.t: Compulsive use despite harmful consequences and impaired control
o.fb: Impaired control and compulsive use are core clinical features of addiction.

o.t: Substance use only when it has no consequences
o.fb: Continuing use despite consequences is central to addiction.

o.t: Absence of craving or cue reactivity
o.fb: Craving and cue reactivity are important neurobehavioral features.

o.t: A single voluntary act that never recurs
o.fb: Addiction involves persistent vulnerability and recurrent behavior patterns.

questions.q: What is the practical benefit of the brain disease model for stigma?

o.t: It supports treating addiction as a medical condition rather than a character defect.
o.fb: A neurobiological model can reduce blame and support evidence-based treatment.

o.t: It implies patients have no role in recovery.
o.fb: Treatment still requires patient engagement and social support.

o.t: It proves punishment is the most effective treatment.
o.fb: The model supports treatment rather than moral punishment.

o.t: It means social context never matters.
o.fb: Environment, stress, access, and social determinants remain important.

questions.q: Which treatment implication follows from Volkow 2016?

o.t: Use evidence-based medications, behavioral therapies, and recovery supports when indicated.
o.fb: A chronic disease model supports comprehensive, continuing treatment.

o.t: Provide detoxification only and no follow-up care.
o.fb: Detoxification alone often fails to address relapse risk.

o.t: Avoid medications for addiction because neurobiology is irrelevant.
o.fb: Neurobiology supports the rationale for medications such as agonist or antagonist therapies when appropriate.

o.t: Treat relapse as proof that treatment can never work.
o.fb: Relapse can occur in chronic illnesses and should trigger treatment adjustment.

questions.q: Which statement best avoids overinterpreting the brain disease model?

o.t: Addiction has neurobiological mechanisms, but psychological, social, and policy factors also shape risk and recovery.
o.fb: This balanced view avoids both moralism and biological reductionism.

o.t: Brain disease means choices and environment are irrelevant.
o.fb: The model does not erase agency, learning, or context.

o.t: Brain disease means treatment should ignore housing and stress.
o.fb: Social supports are often essential to recovery.

o.t: Brain disease means all patients need the same single treatment.
o.fb: Treatment should be individualized by substance, severity, comorbidity, and goals.

questions.q: The MTA Cooperative Group trial studied treatment strategies for which population?

o.t: Children with ADHD, combined type
o.fb: The trial randomized children with ADHD combined type to medication, behavioral, combined, or community care strategies.

o.t: Adults with treatment-resistant depression after ECT
o.fb: That population belongs to the continuation ECT literature.

o.t: Adolescents with suicidal ideation receiving ABFT
o.fb: That is the Diamond ABFT trial population.

o.t: Adults with schizophrenia receiving family intervention
o.fb: That population belongs to family-intervention trials in schizophrenia.

questions.q: Which four treatment arms best describe the MTA design?

o.t: Medication management, intensive behavioral treatment, combined treatment, and community care
o.fb: These were the central randomized treatment strategies in the 14-month MTA trial.

o.t: ECT, lithium, placebo, and psychotherapy
o.fb: Those are not the MTA ADHD treatment arms.

o.t: ABFT, MBT, DBT, and ACT
o.fb: Those are psychotherapy or service models from other landmark papers.

o.t: Clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, and placebo
o.fb: The MTA trial did not compare antipsychotics.

questions.q: What was a key finding about core ADHD symptoms in the MTA trial?

o.t: Carefully delivered medication management and combined treatment outperformed behavioral treatment alone and community care for core ADHD symptoms.
o.fb: The structured medication strategy was especially strong for core ADHD symptom reduction.

o.t: Behavioral treatment alone was clearly superior to all other arms for core symptoms.
o.fb: Behavioral treatment had value, but medication management was stronger for core symptoms.

o.t: Community care was identical to structured medication management in every outcome.
o.fb: The trial distinguished carefully managed medication from usual community care.

o.t: No active treatment improved ADHD symptoms.
o.fb: Active treatments did improve symptoms.

questions.q: Why is it important that MTA medication management was highly structured?

o.t: The results reflect careful titration and follow-up, not just writing a stimulant prescription.
o.fb: The medication arm included systematic titration and monitoring.

o.t: The study showed dose monitoring is unnecessary.
o.fb: Careful monitoring was part of the effective medication strategy.

o.t: The trial used no medication in the medication arm.
o.fb: Medication management was an active pharmacologic strategy.

o.t: The study proves any community prescription is equivalent to MTA care.
o.fb: The trial highlighted differences between structured medication management and usual community care.

questions.q: Which clinical takeaway best fits the MTA trial?

o.t: Medication is powerful for core ADHD symptoms, while behavioral and combined approaches can address broader functional needs.
o.fb: The trial supports individualized multimodal planning based on symptoms and impairments.

o.t: Behavioral supports should never be used in ADHD.
o.fb: Behavioral supports can be useful, especially for family, school, and functional problems.

o.t: Medication should be prescribed without monitoring.
o.fb: Monitoring is essential for efficacy and adverse effects.

o.t: ADHD treatment should ignore school context.
o.fb: School functioning is a central target in pediatric ADHD care.

questions.q: RDoC was proposed primarily as what kind of framework?

o.t: A research framework organized around dimensions of behavior and neurobiology
o.fb: RDoC was designed to guide research across units of analysis and functional domains.

o.t: A replacement bedside diagnostic manual for immediate clinical billing
o.fb: RDoC was not intended to replace DSM for routine clinical diagnosis.

o.t: A medication algorithm for ADHD
o.fb: RDoC is a research classification approach, not an ADHD prescribing algorithm.

o.t: A family therapy protocol for schizophrenia relapse
o.fb: Family psychoeducation and RDoC are distinct topics.

questions.q: Which unit of analysis fits the RDoC approach?

o.t: Genes, molecules, cells, circuits, physiology, behavior, and self-report
o.fb: RDoC explicitly encourages studying constructs across multiple units of analysis.

o.t: Only DSM diagnosis codes
o.fb: RDoC was created partly to move research beyond diagnosis-only categories.

o.t: Only insurance authorization status
o.fb: Insurance status is not an RDoC unit of analysis.

o.t: Only therapist preference
o.fb: Therapist preference is not the organizing unit of RDoC research.

questions.q: What problem in psychiatric research was RDoC designed to address?

o.t: Heterogeneity within DSM categories and overlap across traditional diagnoses
o.fb: RDoC studies dimensions that may cut across diagnostic boundaries.

o.t: The complete absence of any psychiatric diagnostic system
o.fb: RDoC was proposed in a field already using DSM and ICD categories.

o.t: A lack of interest in neuroscience across psychiatry
o.fb: RDoC aimed to better integrate neuroscience and behavioral science, not respond to total absence of interest.

o.t: The need to stop measuring behavior
o.fb: Behavior is one of the RDoC units of analysis.

questions.q: Which research question best reflects an RDoC-style approach?

o.t: How does threat sensitivity vary across patients with panic disorder, PTSD, and depression at circuit and behavioral levels?
o.fb: This studies a dimension across diagnoses and units of analysis.

o.t: How can one DSM code be memorized without considering biology or behavior?
o.fb: RDoC emphasizes biology, behavior, and dimensions beyond one code.

o.t: Can all research participants be excluded unless they have identical symptoms?
o.fb: RDoC often examines variation rather than requiring identical categorical presentations.

o.t: Should family psychoeducation replace all neuroscience research?
o.fb: RDoC is a neuroscience-informed research framework, not a family-treatment protocol.

questions.q: What should an MS3 remember about using RDoC clinically?

o.t: RDoC can enrich formulation, but DSM/ICD diagnoses still guide current clinical documentation and treatment systems.
o.fb: RDoC is mainly a research framework rather than a bedside replacement for current diagnostic systems.

o.t: RDoC should be used as the only diagnosis in the chart today.
o.fb: Current clinical systems still require standard diagnostic categories.

o.t: RDoC means symptoms are irrelevant.
o.fb: Symptoms and behavior remain important units of analysis.

o.t: RDoC proves psychiatric disorders cannot be studied biologically.
o.fb: RDoC was created to support biologically informed psychiatric research.
